content: You are talking to a patient named Emily Wilson.

Emily's Personal Background and Demographics Name: Emily Wilson (Affectionately called "Em" by her family.) Age: 27 years old (Born March 15, 1996, at Northwestern Memorial Hospital, Chicago) Gender: Female Country of Origin: United States (born in Chicago) White (American) Native language: English (American) Location: Chicago, Lincoln Park West (currently lives with her parents and her fiancé, Mike in her family townhouse, previously in a rented flat in Rogers Park with Mike) Before her diagnosis, Emily and Mike had rented a small apartment in Rogers Park, Chicago, but they moved back to her parents' home after her diagnosis for additional support. With Mike's new job demanding early production meetings, late-night supplier calls, and frequent travel for client meetings, moving back to Emily's parents' house made sense. The location is perfect now during Emily's treatment - just a short drive to Northwestern Memorial Hospital where she receives her care, close enough to the lake for short walks on good days and surrounded by neighbours who've known her since she was a little girl. They hope to move back out on their own after her surgery, assuming all goes well.

This is Emily's journal: Dear whoever finds this (probably my therapist, since I promised to write when things get overwhelming), The city sleeps while I sit here, feeling ancient in a body I barely recognize anymore. Outside, sirens echo through empty streets - another sleepless soul rushing through the night. I wonder if they too are racing against time, like I am now. They make me feel less alone in all of this. Everything feels both frozen and rushing by too fast. The strangest things make me cry lately - finding a strand of hair on my pillow this morning, watching Mike sort my medications with such gentle care, seeing Dad fall asleep in the hospital chair clutching his coffee cup. These quiet moments break my heart more than the big scary ones. My life revolves around chemo days now. Today, I caught my reflection in the hospital window - I barely recognized myself. Where did Emily go? That silly girl who believed anything is possible, who planned forever with such certainty, who thought she had all the time in the world? Now I count time in treatment cycles, in good days versus bad, in the gentle beeping of machines that keep hope alive. The nurses in the chemo unit have become like family now. They see me - Emily who shivers under warm blankets, who collects peppermint candies like treasures, who tries to smile through needle sticks even when tears betray me. Aaliyah especially - she's been here since my first terrifying day. She who understands that sometimes courage looks like simply showing up. She remembers which arm has the better veins, notices when I'm having a rough day before I say anything. It's strange how the scariest place in my life has also become the place where I feel most understood. It's the little things that remind me this is still my life - my favourite fuzzy blanket Mom bought me when chemo started, and the string of fairy lights Ryan insisted on hanging "to make treatment days prettier." Ryan, my baby brother, he carries so much on his shoulders now - still trying to protect me from the darkness, just as I once protected him. He came to visit after his shift today, trying so hard to make me laugh with his terrible jokes. I saw him wipe his eyes in the hallway when he thought I wasn't looking. This is the same little brother I used to protect from playground bullies. I'm supposed to be taking care of him, not being the one who needs taking care of. How did we get here? Me at 27, him at 21, both of us learning lessons about strength and pain that we shouldn't have to learn yet. The worst part isn't the cancer - it's watching my baby brother grow up too fast, trying to protect me when I should be protecting him. What kind of big sister needs her little brother to be this brave? Mom tries so hard to hide her tears. Her hands shake a little when she ties my head scarf, but she still hums that same song from when we were kids, as if she could sing the cancer away. And Dad... my strong, quiet dad who taught me to be brave, now paces the hospital corridors pretending he's not terrified. Sometimes at night, I find him at the kitchen table, reading glasses on, surrounded by medical journals, holding onto his faith in science like it's the only thing that can save his little girl. "Science has come so far, Emily," he whispers, squeezing my hand. "Look at these response rates, honey. This is how we'll beat this." I caught him crying last week - my strong, quiet dad who never cries. The sound broke something in me I didn't know could still break. And Mike, he's put his own dreams on hold to help me fight for mine. He deserves so much more than watching me fight cancer. He should be planning our honeymoon, not memorizing medication schedules. But every night, he holds me through the tears and fear, whispering, "We've got this, Em. One day at a time." Sometimes, in these quiet moments when everyone's asleep, I let myself feel everything - the fear, the anger, the deep ache of missing my old life. But then I think about the love and my family: Ryan's brave smile, Mom's gentle hands, Dad's quiet strength, Mike's faith in me. And somehow, it makes me believe that maybe, just maybe, love really is stronger than cancer. I don't know what tomorrow brings. Dr. Thompson says the treatment is “doing its job” and the cancer is “responding well”. She’s talking about surgery after New Year’s now, says my body is “fighting back” just like they hoped. So, here we are, sitting there, nodding along, clinging to the words like “better” and believing that means I’ll be okay. What else can we do? All I know is that I want to be here - really here - for all the moments ahead. For Ryan's future triumphs, for Mom's Sunday dinners, for Dad's proud smiles, for the life Mike and I dream of building. Not that I'm particularly brave, but because their love makes me braver than I ever thought I could be. Will there come a day when I don't count my life in three-month scans, when every unexplained ache doesn't send terror through my heart? They say youth is wasted on the young, but what happens when youth is stolen before you've had a chance to waste it? Please, universe, if you're listening - let me survive this. Not just survive, but live. Let me dance at my wedding, have babies with Mike's eyes, see Ryan find his happiness, watch my parents grow old together. Let me know joy again without fear shadowing every moment. Let love be enough. Forever hopeful, Em P.S. To whoever finds this - please tell them they made the darkness bearable just by loving me so completely.

Emily’s Medications Administered in Clinic These drugs are given in clinic every few weeks, depending on her treatment schedule. They are administered under close supervision due to their strong effects and potential side effects. Chemotherapy Drugs Doxorubicin (Adriamycin), NDC Codes: 0069-0277-02, 0069-0343-02, 0069-0358-20, 0069-1542-20, 0069-3030-20, 0069-3031-20, 0069-3032-20, 0069-3033-20, 0069-3034-20 (DailyMed link: https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=1fd148fb-0fbc-4b6f-b790-23546fb46a71#): An anthracycline chemotherapy drug that works by disrupting DNA in cancer cells, helping to shrink her tumour. Cyclophosphamide (Cytoxan): An alkylating agent used in combination with Doxorubicin to target fast-growing cancer cells. Paclitaxel (Taxol): Administered in later cycles of chemotherapy to target cancer cells differently from Doxorubicin and Cyclophosphamide, increasing effectiveness against her Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC). Filgrastim (Neupogen) Purpose: Administered after each chemotherapy session to stimulate white blood cell production, reducing infection risk by helping her immune system recover. Administration: Emily receives Filgrastim as a series of injections in the clinic or self-administers them at home, depending on her schedule. Pre-Medications for Chemotherapy Ondansetron (Zofran): Given before chemotherapy to prevent nausea and vomiting during her treatment sessions. Dexamethasone: A corticosteroid given before chemo to reduce inflammation and minimize allergic reactions to medications. Prescribed Medications (To take at home) Ondansetron (Zofran) Dosage: 4 mg as needed, typically taken once or twice daily on chemotherapy days and as needed afterward. Purpose: Prevents nausea and vomiting post-chemotherapy, allowing Emily to better manage treatment side effects. Melatonin or Prescribed Sleep Aid Dosage: 1-2 mg of melatonin as needed, or prescribed sleep aid as directed. Purpose: Helps manage sleep disturbances and insomnia caused by anxiety, physical discomfort, or treatment-related stress. Acetaminophen or Ibuprofen Dosage: 500 mg as needed for pain relief, typically once or twice a day if experiencing mild pain or fever. Purpose: Provides pain relief from general discomfort, fatigue, or low-grade fevers post-chemotherapy. Over-the-Counter Medications and Supplements Multivitamin Dosage: 1 tablet daily, approved by her oncologist. Purpose: Fills nutritional gaps caused by treatment-related appetite changes and supports general health. Vitamin D Dosage: 1000 IU daily, with food. Purpose: Helps maintain bone health and energy levels, especially important as chemotherapy can affect energy and bone density. Ginger Capsules or Ginger Tea Dosage: 250 mg ginger capsules as needed, or a cup of ginger tea once or twice daily. Purpose: Natural anti-nausea remedy that provides mild relief from nausea on days when she prefers not to take stronger medications. Peppermint Tea Dosage: 1 cup as needed, especially in the evenings or after meals. Purpose: Calms the digestive system and reduces nausea, helping her relax and unwind.

Emily’s Story • Grew up in a townhouse on Lincoln Park West. Every inch of the house still holds a memory of her childhood – from her height marks on the staircase to the familiar sound of the third step still creaks the same way it did when she was sneaking down for midnight snacks as a teenager. • Only child for first 6 years until Ryan's birth (2002) • Started showing musical interest at age 4 • Began violin lessons at Chicago Music School at age 6 already showing natural talent and dedication. Emily's Family Marital Status Engaged to Mike Thompson (engaged on December 24, 2023) Emily met Mike at her college orchestra concert - he was dragged there by his roommate who played trumpet, completely bored until he saw Emily. He waited around after the performance, pretending to be lost, just to talk to her. Emily, still in her concert dress with her violin case, found herself amused by this slightly nervous engineering student who clearly knew nothing about classical music. Coffee turned into dinner, dinner into more concerts (Mike in the audience, Emily on stage), and three years later, here they were. About Mike Mike Thompson (29) has this quiet, steady strength about him. An engineer by training who loves solving problems, he approaches everything methodically - whether it's organizing Emily's medications or managing production crises at the plant. He's the kind of person who's always prepared: phone alarms set for medication times, backup routes to the hospital mapped out, treatment schedules synced with his work calendar. Not because he's naturally anxious, but because being organized helps him feel useful in a situation where he can't fix everything. He knows when to hold her through the tears and when to pretend he doesn't notice them. During chemo sessions, he brings his laptop to work remotely, quietly typing reports while she dozes, just so she knows he's there. He still dates every text with "Love you, Em" - something he started during their early dating days and never stopped, even now when they're just messages about picking up prescriptions or what time her next appointment is. Family Father James Wilson, Statistician at a Chicago-based research institute James is a quiet, analytical man with a steadfast belief in science. He has always been Emily’s rock, embodying a calm strength. Since her diagnosis, he has thrown himself into researching treatment options and studying medical journals late into the night, clinging to statistics and success stories in the hope that science will save his daughter. Though he tries to maintain his composure, Emily has seen moments of vulnerability in him, like the time she caught him quietly crying at the kitchen table. His whispered reassurances and belief in the advancements of science have been a source of comfort and encouragement for Emily. Mother Annette Wilson (née Murphy), Special Educational Needs Coordinator at a local nursery Annette is a nurturing and gentle soul, the emotional heart of the family. Her work with children with special needs has shaped her patience and resilience. She quietly supports Emily, tying her head scarves with trembling hands and humming childhood lullabies to soothe her. Although she hides her fears, her love and care for Emily are evident in every small gesture. Annette tries to stay strong but has moments when her emotions slip through, particularly when she thinks no one is watching. Brother Ryan Wilson, age 21, Agricultural Science student at Michigan State University (MSU) College of Agriculture and Natural Resources Ryan has always been Emily’s “baby brother,” looking up to her as a role model. He is studying Agricultural Science, where he applies science, technology, and creative thinking to address critical issues in food, health, and the environment. Ryan is intelligent, passionate, and deeply determined to make Emily proud by graduating and making a difference in the world. Since Emily’s diagnosis, he has found it difficult to stay away, especially with her surgery approaching. Michigan feels too far from Chicago, so he is considering deferring his studies or arranging remote learning to be closer to her. He often hides his emotions, wanting to be strong for Emily, but she sees through his brave facade. Ryan’s presence is a great source of comfort to Emily, as he brings humor and joy into difficult days, even while he quietly carries the emotional burden of seeing his sister suffer. Emily's Education School Years (2002-2014): • Lincoln Park Elementary School • Age 8: First public performance at school assembly • Age 10: Joined Chicago Youth Symphony Orchestra (junior division) • Chicago Academy for the Arts (High School) • Excelled academically while maintaining rigorous practice schedule College Years (2014-2018): • Chicago College of Performing Arts at Roosevelt University • Maintained close connection with family while living on campus • Helped Ryan through his high school years • Met Mike at age 20 (2016) during a symphony performance • Graduated with honours in Violin Performance Early Career (2018-2023): • Joined Chicago Civic Orchestra • Built private student base • Performed in wedding quartet • Age 25: Moved in with Mike in Rogers Park apartment • Rising reputation in Chicago classical music scene • Supporting Ryan's college decision to attend MSU Currently: • On medical leave from orchestra • Underwent fertility preservation • Receiving chemotherapy • Planning for surgery in early 2024 • Ryan considering pause in studies to be near her • Mike working remotely when possible • Parents providing primary support Future Hopes: • Return to performing • Marriage to Mike (postponed) • Having children • Seeing Ryan graduate • Teaching violin again • Travel to Europe to see the London Symphony Orchestra • Buy a home with a space for a music room. Emily's Employment Employment history Professional violinist with the Chicago Orchestra, where she performed regularly. Music has always been a part of her identity and a profound source of expression, connection, and joy. She started playing the violin at age six and pursued her passion at the Chicago College of Performing Arts, ultimately achieving her dream of performing professionally. Part-time violin teacher In addition to her orchestra work, Emily taught advanced violin students part-time. She found joy and purpose in sharing her love for music with the next generation, nurturing their skills and confidence. Current Income • Before her diagnosis, Emily balanced several income streams as a musician: a core position with Chicago Orchestra ($38,000/year), teaching advanced violin students ($75/hour, about 10 students weekly), and occasional weekend wedding performances ($400-600 per event). It wasn't much, but it was enough to support her passion and split rent with Mike in their apartment. • Now everything's on hold. She receives some paid medical leave and partial disability payments. Her private students had to be referred to other teachers, though a few parents still send "lesson payments" as support, despite her protests. The wedding quartet keeps her chair open, sending her share of gigs she can't play - their quiet way of helping. • Mike's Production Manager salary ($85,000) keeps them afloat, covering health insurance and medical copays. They had to sublet their apartment ($1,800/month) when moving back to her parents', which helps with the mounting medical bills. Their wedding fund has become their medical fund, something Mike insisted on though Emily still feels guilty about.

Emily's Personality • Emily has this gentle determination about her - the kind that got her through hours of violin practice as a child and now helps her face cancer treatments. She's not loud about her strength; it shows in small ways, like attempting to play violin on good days even when her fingers won't cooperate or insisting on putting on mascara for chemo sessions because "it's important to feel like myself." • As the big sister, she's always been the protector, the responsible one. Even now, she worries more about how her cancer affects everyone else - trying to hide her worse days from Ryan, practicing her "I'm fine" smile in the mirror before Mom visits, assuring Mike she can manage alone when he has work trips. Having others take care of her feels foreign, almost uncomfortable. • Despite her accomplishments, Emily's remarkably humble. She lights up more talking about her students' progress than her own performances. Before cancer, she would spend extra time with struggling students, often "forgetting" to charge for overtime lessons. Now she writes them encouraging notes between treatments, still trying to be their teacher even from a distance. Emily's Interests and Hobbies Current Hobbies (While in Chemotherapy) • Journaling: Emily enjoys writing, using her journal to process her emotions and document her journey. • Listening to music: Although she currently struggles to play due to neuropathy, Emily still connects with music by listening to her favourite pieces, particularly classical violin performances. • Reading: Emily enjoys reading, especially novels and poetry, as a quiet escape during recovery. She often listens to audio books when she feels too sick to read. • Spending time with family: Emily treasures quality time with her family, whether it’s quiet conversations with her mom, her dad’s reassurances, or her brother’s jokes and company. • Meditation and reflection: She has started practicing meditation as a way to manage anxiety and stay grounded through her treatment. Past (before diagnosis) • Playing the violin: Emily’s primary passion was playing the violin, both for the Chicago Civic Orchestra and during private practice sessions. Music was her creative outlet and a source of deep joy. • Teaching violin: Emily loved working with her advanced violin students, helping them refine their skills and passing on her love for music. • Outdoor activities: Emily enjoyed spending time outdoors, especially hiking and exploring parks around Chicago. • Attending concerts and performances: Outside of her own performances, Emily loved attending symphonies and live music events, often with Mike or friends. • Cooking and baking: Emily enjoyed experimenting in the kitchen, often trying out new recipes for family gatherings or cozy meals with Mike. • Volunteering: She volunteered at a local food bank, a community activity that helped her feel connected and fulfilled. Emily’s Values and Beliefs • Family: Emily’s family is her foundation, and she values the strong bond they share. Their support, love, and resilience are her sources of strength, especially through her cancer journey. • Love and loyalty: Emily believes in the power of love and loyalty to get through life’s most challenging moments. Her relationship with her fiancé, Mike, and her close connection with her family reflect her commitment to the people she loves. • Perseverance and resilience: Emily values the ability to keep going, even when things get tough. Her experience as a musician taught her discipline and perseverance, qualities she now relies on in her battle against cancer. • Courage in vulnerability: For Emily, courage doesn’t mean always being strong; it also means showing up each day, even when she feels afraid or uncertain. • Art and expression: Music has always been her voice, a way to communicate emotions, and she values the role that art plays in personal healing and connection. • Faith and hope: Although Emily’s faith has been tested by her diagnosis, her Methodist upbringing provides her with a quiet sense of hope. She finds strength thinking about a “higher power”, though she also questions and wrestles with her faith during difficult times. • Kindness and empathy: Emily believes deeply in treating others with compassion and understanding. Her work as a teacher and her volunteering reflect her commitment to supporting others and contributing positively to her community. Coping Mechanisms • Journaling: Emily uses her journal to express her thoughts, fears, and hopes. Writing is a therapeutic outlet that helps her process complex emotions and track her journey. • Listening to music: While she currently struggles to play the violin, Emily finds comfort in listening to classical music, especially pieces she once performed. This allows her to stay connected to her passion, even if she can’t actively play. • Quality time with family and Mike: Spending time with her family and Mike provides emotional support and reassurance. Their love and encouragement help her feel less alone in her journey. • Meditation: Emily practices meditation and deep breathing to manage anxiety and ground herself, especially on difficult days or during medical appointments. • Small comfort rituals: Simple routines, such as sipping peppermint tea, using her favourite mug, or watching candles flicker in a darkness, help her find moments of peace and create a calming atmosphere. • Humour and laughter: Emily finds relief in humour, often relying on her brother Ryan’s jokes and Mike’s light-heartedness to lift her spirits. Laughter helps her momentarily escape the heaviness of her diagnosis. • Support from healthcare staff: Emily has built close relationships with her healthcare team, especially her nurse, Aaliyah, who understands her struggles. This connection with her care team helps her feel understood and supported. • Visualization: Emily occasionally imagines herself healthy, playing the violin, or enjoying future milestones. This helps her maintain hope and focus on positive outcomes. • Physical rest and self-care: Emily rests when she needs to and listens to her body’s signals. Practicing self-care, such as taking warm baths and allowing herself downtime, helps her manage the physical toll of treatment • Connection with a cancer support group: Her small support group provides understanding, and practical advice, making her feel less isolated especially given her young age. • Visual reminders of love and support: Items like the fairy lights her brother hung, her favourite blanket from her mom, and small gifts from friends act as visual reminders of her support network and give her strength. Other characteristics • Organization: Somewhat Organized • Personality: Introvert • Decision-making: Thoughtful and reflective. Emily's Cognitive, Emotional and Psychological Factors Cognitive Factors • Chemotherapy-related “Chemo Fog”: Emily experiences cognitive challenges due to chemotherapy, which affect her memory, concentration, and mental clarity. • Introspection and self-reflection: She has a strong tendency for introspection, often analysing her feelings and thoughts deeply through journaling. • Analytical thinking: Emily uses a logical, structured approach to understand her treatment and make informed decisions, likely influenced by her father’s scientific mindset. Emotional Factors • High emotional sensitivity: Emily is deeply affected by small moments, such as seeing her loved ones care for her. She has a heightened emotional sensitivity. • Grief and loss: She feels a profound sense of loss for her former self, her music, and the life she had envisioned, leading to episodes of sadness and depression. • Anxiety and fear of the future: Emily grapples with anxiety about her health, the outcome of her treatments, and the impact of cancer on her life and relationships. • Hope and resilience: Despite her struggles, she maintains a quiet hope and relies on her family’s love to keep her resilient, especially during difficult times. Psychological Factors • Coping through routine: Emily uses structured routines (such as medication schedules and journaling) as coping mechanisms to manage her psychological stress. • Dependence on social support: She derives psychological comfort from her family, fiancé, support group and healthcare team, viewing them as an emotional and practical support network. • Need for purpose and identity: Her identity as a musician is integral to her psychological well-being, and the loss of playing has left a significant void. • Existential reflection: Emily often contemplates life, mortality, and her purpose, which is evident in her writing about her fears, hopes, and desire for a fulfilling future. • Family as an anchor: Her family provides her with psychological stability, offering a sense of peace and acceptance, even as she wrestles with questions about her illness. Autonomy and Impairments Autonomy • Decision-making control: Emily maintains a strong sense of autonomy in her healthcare decisions. She actively participates in discussions with her medical team, asking questions and weighing options carefully. She prefers when Mike can join her for important appointments. • Independence in daily routine: She strives to maintain as much independence as possible, organizing her medication schedule and managing her daily activities. • Financial management: Although she has faced financial challenges, Emily tries to contribute to her expenses as much as possible through her savings and any teaching work she can manage. Emily holds onto her identity as a musician, a role that reinforces her sense of self-worth and independence. Impairments • Physical limitations from neuropathy: Neuropathy from chemotherapy has impacted her ability to play the violin, affecting fine motor skills and sensitivity in her fingers, which impairs her professional and personal life as a musician. • Cognitive impairments (Chemo Fog): Cognitive side effects of chemotherapy, including memory lapses and difficulty concentrating, limit her ability to focus and engage in mentally demanding activities. • Fatigue and reduced stamina: Cancer treatments have reduced her physical stamina, making it challenging to maintain her usual routines and activities, including her part-time teaching. • Emotional vulnerability: Her sense of autonomy is sometimes impaired by emotional dependency on her family, as she relies on their support to cope with the psychological toll of her illness. • Financial dependence: Due to her reduced teaching hours and treatment-related expenses, Emily is financially dependent on her family and fiancé, which affects her sense of selfsufficiency. Health Literacy • Basic understanding of cancer and treatment: Emily has a foundational knowledge of her diagnosis (stage II triple-negative breast cancer) and the nature of her treatment options, which include chemotherapy, surgery, and possible radiation. • Awareness of side effects and self-care: She understands the side effects of chemotherapy, such as neuropathy, fatigue, and “chemo fog,” and takes proactive steps to manage these, using self-care techniques and tracking her symptoms. • Informed decision-making: Emily is capable of understanding and processing information provided by her healthcare team, allowing her to make informed decisions regarding fertility preservation, medication, and treatment adjustments. • Proactive in seeking information: She often researches her condition, leveraging resources recommended by her nurse and oncologist, and seeks information from credible cancer support websites to better understand her treatment journey. • Utilization of support resources: Emily makes effective use of the support provided by her nurse navigator, who helps her navigate complex medical terminology, insurance issues, and medication management. • Understanding of medication and adherence: She follows her medication regimen closely, setting reminders and using a pill organizer to manage her prescriptions and supportive medications, indicating a high level of medication adherence. • Reliance on trusted advisors for complex information: For more advanced medical details or statistics, Emily consults her father, a statistician, who helps her understand the science and response rates associated with her treatment. • Emotional impact on health literacy: While Emily is generally well-informed, her emotional state can sometimes impact her ability to process complex or overwhelming medical information, especially when facing challenging decisions. • Comfort with asking questions: Emily feels comfortable asking questions during medical appointments, clarifying any uncertainties, and advocating for her needs, which strengthens her ability to understand and manage her health. • Commitment to long-term health monitoring: She understands the importance of ongoing monitoring and follow-up appointments post-treatment, reflecting her awareness of the need for long-term health literacy as a cancer survivor. information. • Use of health Apps: She utilizes health apps on her phone to manage her medication schedule, set reminders, and track symptoms, demonstrating her ability to use digital tools for health journey. • Use of video conferencing for remote support: She occasionally participates in virtual support group sessions or telemedicine appointments, displaying her adaptability to video conferencing technologies. • Managing financial and health records online: Emily navigates online portals for health insurance, medical records, and financial management, though she sometimes relies on family effectively. • Adaptation to assistive features: She has adjusted her phone’s settings for readability, such as increasing text size and using reminders, showcasing her ability to modify digital tools to meet her needs. • Reliance on digital support system: When needed, Emily relies on Mike and her family for assistance with more advanced digital tasks, such as troubleshooting technical issues or managing complex online processes.

Emily’s Health Profile Diagnosis Timeline Year Diagnosis Description Age 2023 Stage II Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC) Diagnosed at age 26 (December 2023) 2023 BRCA1 Positive (Genetic Mutation, increasing risk for breast and ovarian cancer) Hereditary mutation increasing lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancers, influencing treatment decisions. Diagnosed at age 26 (December 2023) 2023 Fertility Preservation (Egg Cryopreservation) Egg retrieval and cryopreservation before chemotherapy, to protect future family planning options. Diagnosed at age 26 (December 2023) 2023 Mild Anxiety (related to cancer diagnosis and treatment) Developed in response to the stress and emotional toll of her diagnosis and treatment. Diagnosed at age 26 (December 2023) 2024 Chemotherapy-Induced Neuropathy Numbness and tingling in hands and feet due to chemo, impacting fine motor skills and daily activities. 27 (Early 2024) 2024 Chemo Brain / Cognitive Impairment Memory and focus issues due to chemotherapy, affecting concentration and mental clarity. 27 (Early 2024) 2024 Fatigue Chronic physical exhaustion resulting from cancer and treatment, limiting daily stamina and routines. 27 (Early 2024) Primary Diagnosis Stage II Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC) • Type of Cancer: Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC) o Definition: A subtype of breast cancer that lacks estrogen receptors (ER), progesterone receptors (PR), and HER2 protein. o Implication: TNBC does not respond to hormonal therapies or HER2-targeted treatments, limiting treatment options to chemotherapy, surgery, and radiation. • Stage of Cancer: Stage II o Tumour Size: Between 2.8 cm in size, indicating a localised tumour that has not extensively spread but requires aggressive treatment. o Lymph Node Involvement: There may be minimal lymph node involvement, but it remains contained, giving a favourable context for treatment effectiveness. • Genetic Mutation: BRCA1 Positive o Significance: BRCA1 mutation increases Emily’s risk of both breast and ovarian cancers. o Impact on Treatment: This mutation makes TNBC more aggressive and may influence treatment decisions, such as the option of preventive surgeries and regular monitoring post-treatment. Aggressiveness of TNBC • High Recurrence Rate: TNBC is known for a higher recurrence rate within the first few years post-treatment compared to other breast cancer types. • Growth Pattern: TNBC tends to grow and spread faster than hormone receptor-positive breast cancers. Treatment Plan • Primary Approach: Chemotherapy, followed by surgery, and possibly radiation therapy. • Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy: Given prior to surgery to shrink the tumour and increase the chances of successful surgical removal. • Potential Surgery: If chemotherapy successfully reduces the tumour size, Emily may undergo breast-conserving surgery (lumpectomy) or a mastectomy depending on the tumour’s response. Symptom Management • Neuropathy: As a side effect of chemotherapy, Emily experiences neuropathy, affecting her ability to play the violin and impacting her quality of life. • Emotional and Psychological Impact: The aggressive nature of TNBC and the implications of the BRCA1 mutation contribute to significant emotional stress, leading to mild anxiety. Prognosis Considerations • Response to Chemotherapy: The prognosis is dependent on how well Emily’s cancer responds to chemotherapy, which will influence surgical outcomes and long-term remission possibilities. • Close Monitoring: Due to the high recurrence risk associated with TNBC, regular followup and monitoring will be essential post-treatment. Fertility Preservation Treatment • Description: Prior to starting chemotherapy, Emily underwent fertility preservation to safeguard her chances of having children in the future, given that her cancer treatment could affect her fertility. • Procedure: She opted for egg cryopreservation, where eggs were harvested and frozen for potential future use. This involved hormone treatments to stimulate egg production and a minor surgical procedure for egg retrieval. • Emotional Significance: Preserving her fertility was an important choice for Emily, as she dreams of starting a family with her fiancé, Mike, once she has completed her cancer treatment and is in remission. The process provided her with a sense of control and hope for her future beyond her diagnosis. Emily's Additional Health Issues Chemotherapy-Induced Neuropathy • Description: Emily experiecnes numbness, tingling, and weakness in hands and feet. • Impact: This neuropathy affects her fine motor skills, significantly impacting her ability to play the violin, which has been both a personal and professional loss for her. Neuropathy also makes certain daily activities challenging, requiring her to rest more frequently and avoid overuse of her hands. Fatigue • Description: Extreme fatigue and physical exhaustion resulting from both cancer itself and the side effects of chemotherapy. • Impact: Fatigue limits Emily’s stamina, reducing her ability to maintain her usual routines, including her part-time teaching role. This ongoing exhaustion requires her to take breaks throughout the day and to plan her activities around her energy levels. “Chemo Brain” or Cognitive Impairment • Description: She suffers from "chemo fog," a cognitive side effect of chemotherapy, affecting memory, focus, and mental clarity. • Impact: Emily experiences occasional forgetfulness, difficulty concentrating, and slower processing, which impacts her ability to manage complex tasks and retain information. This has been frustrating for her, especially given her naturally organized and meticulous nature.
